sections.title: Enrolling in an evening pottery class
sections.context: You will hear a woman phoning an arts centre in Bristol to enrol on a pottery course.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Harbourside Arts Centre, Owen speaking. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Hello. I saw a poster for your evening pottery classes, and I'd like to sign up for one, if there are any places left.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: There might be. Let me open the enrolment form. Can I take your name?

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Yes, it's Nadia Szymanski.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: I'm sorry, could you spell the surname for me?

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Everyone asks! It's S-Z-Y-M-A-N-S-K-I. Szymanski.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: S-Z-Y-M-A-N-S-K-I. Got it, thank you. Now, which course were you thinking of? We run a wheel throwing course and a hand building course, and both are for beginners.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: I'd really like the wheel, because I've always wanted to make bowls on one of those spinning wheels.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: I'm afraid the wheel course is full until the spring. There's a waiting list, if you'd like me to add you to it. Hand building still has a few places. You make things from coils and slabs of clay, and a lot of people find it easier to begin with.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Well, in that case I'll take hand building, and I can try the wheel later on.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Wonderful. The class is on Tuesday evenings, from seven until nine.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Oh dear. I work late on Tuesdays. Is there any other evening?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Let me look. Yes, there's a second group on Wednesday evenings, at the same times. I can put you in that one.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Wednesday is perfect.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Lovely. The Wednesday course starts on 14 January and runs for ten weeks. There are twelve people in each group, so you'll get plenty of attention from the tutor.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: And how much is it?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: The standard fee is £180. But if you join the centre as a member, which is free for the first year, you get £15 off. So for you it would be £165.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Then I'll join as a member. Is the clay included?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Yes, all the clay, the glazes and the firing are included. The only thing you need to buy is a basic tool kit, with a sponge, a wooden knife and a few other bits. It costs £12, and you pay the tutor in the first week.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: That's fine. Where do the classes take place? I haven't been to the centre before.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: The pottery studio is on the second floor, at the back of the building. The main entrance is on the harbour side, next to the café. There's a lift if you'd rather not use the stairs. The number 5 bus stops right outside, and there's a small car park, although it fills up quickly in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: I'll probably take the bus. Do you need my address?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Yes, please. We send the confirmation by post as well as by email.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: It's 17 Harbour Street, Bristol. Oh, wait. Sorry, that's my old flat. I moved in September. It's 17 Harbour Street, no, I mean 71 Marsh Lane. Sorry, I keep forgetting.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: No problem. So that's 71 Marsh Lane. And the postcode?

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: BS1 5RW. That's B-S-1, then 5-R-W.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: B-S-1, 5-R-W. Thank you. And have you done any pottery before?

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Only once. When I was at school we made a bowl, but it cracked in the kiln. I wasn't very good at it!

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Don't worry, everyone starts somewhere. The tutor, Mrs Patterson, is very patient. One important thing: please bring an apron, because clay gets everywhere, and wear clothes you don't mind getting dirty. You can leave your work on the drying shelves between classes.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: What happens if I miss a class?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Then you can come to a catch-up session on the first Saturday of each month, free of charge. You just need to tell the tutor beforehand. We also have an open studio on Sunday afternoons, if you want extra practice.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: That sounds great. Will we be able to take our pots home?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Yes, in the last week, after they have been fired. Most people leave with four or five pieces.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Brilliant. Do I need to pay today?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: We'll send you a payment link by email within the hour. If you pay in the next two days, your place is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: I'll do that tonight.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Then welcome to the Harbourside Arts Centre, Nadia. We'll see you in January.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Thank you, Owen. Goodbye.

sections.title: A new exhibition at a science centre
sections.context: You will hear a member of staff at a science centre in Dublin welcoming visitors to a new ocean exhibition.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Liffey Science Centre. My name is Aoife, and I'll be introducing our new exhibition, which is called Under the Surface. It's a journey from the sunlit shallows of the ocean to the darkest places on Earth, and I hope you'll enjoy every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Before we go in, let me explain a few practical things. First, opening times. The exhibition is open from ten until five every day. On Thursdays, however, we stay open late. Some of you may have heard that we close at nine on those evenings, but that was only during the opening month. From now on we close at eight o'clock, so please plan your visit accordingly.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Now, about tickets. You can buy a ticket at the desk on the day, but we often sell out of the busiest time slots, so I'd strongly recommend booking online in advance. It's cheaper that way as well, and you can choose your time. If you do arrive without a ticket, we will do our best, but we can't promise.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: A word about photography. You're very welcome to take photographs, and many visitors like to share them on social media. The one thing we ask is that you switch off your flash. Some of our displays include light-sensitive specimens, such as old preserved sea creatures, and a bright flash can damage them over time. Some people believe it disturbs other visitors, and of course that's true, but the real reason is the displays.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Many of you have asked about the audio guide. The good news is that you don't have to pay for it. It's a free app, and you can download it onto your own phone. If you don't have a phone with you, or if you'd like headphones, you can borrow a set from the desk for a small deposit. I'd suggest you download the app before you go in, because the signal inside the building is quite weak.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: One more piece of news. Next month, our planetarium will begin showing a new film about deep sea volcanoes. It's been made by a team of Irish scientists, and it is spectacular. The cinema will stay open at weekends only until the end of the year. So if you'd like to see it, you may want to book a seat now.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Right, let me tell you about the exhibition itself. It's divided into five zones, and you walk through them in order, rather like descending in a submarine.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: The first zone is called the Shallows. This is where most of our younger visitors spend their time, because it's the one place where you can pick things up. There are trays of real shells and sponges and pieces of coral, and you're welcome to touch them. Please wash your hands afterwards, because the basins are just outside.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: The second zone is the Reef. Here we've built a long glass tunnel, and as you walk through it you're surrounded by tanks full of tropical fish. The tank in the middle is home to a small shark, whose name is Murphy. It was named by a school group, and it has been very popular ever since.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Next comes the Twilight Zone, where the light fades away. It's a dark room, and the only sound is the music of the ocean. Here you can sit down and listen to recordings of whales and dolphins that researchers have collected from the Atlantic. Many people tell me this is their favourite part, because it's so peaceful after the busy reef.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Then you arrive in the Deep. The walls are black, and the only light comes from a model of a research submarine. Visitors take turns steering it with a joystick, and the aim is to find a hidden creature on the sea floor. It's much harder than it looks, so don't be disappointed if the submarine gets stuck. You might also be disappointed to hear that the diving suit display is under repair, so you won't be able to try the equipment on this month.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Finally, there's the Lab. It's the last room of the exhibition, and it's where visitors do some of their own science. On the big touch screen, you choose different animals and connect them to build a food chain, from tiny plankton up to the largest whales. If you make a mistake, the screen shows you what would happen to the whole ocean. A lot of adults enjoy this one more than the children do.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: Now, please remember that the exhibition is on one level, and all of the areas are accessible for wheelchairs and buggies. The toilets are near the exit, and the café is on the ground floor. If you'd like to leave a coat or a large bag, the cloakroom is free, and the staff can look after your things until closing time.

transcript.speaker: Aoife
transcript.text: That's everything from me. If you have any questions at all, one of my colleagues in a blue shirt will be happy to help. Thank you for listening, and enjoy Under the Surface.

sections.title: Designing a sleep and memory study
sections.context: You will hear two psychology students discussing a research project on sleep with their tutor.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Come in, Imogen. Hello, Dev. Sit down, and let's talk about your sleep study. I've read your outline, and I have a few questions. First of all, who are your participants?

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: We're planning to use first-year students. We want to find out whether going to bed earlier helps people remember new words.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: And first-years are the easiest group to reach, because we can contact them through the course forum, and the department already has a list of volunteers.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: That's true, but there's another reason. Most of them are about the same age and have similar timetables. That means fewer things that could change the results.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Fair enough. I'd say the second reason is the more convincing one. Convenience is not a scientific argument by itself. Now, I assume you won't be asking them to go to bed at a certain time without checking?

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: No, we'll ask them to keep a sleep diary for two weeks. They write down when they go to bed and when they wake up.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: Last term I did a similar exercise for another module, and the problem was that people forgot to fill the diaries in. They tried to remember everything at the end of the week, and the information wasn't reliable.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: That's why I think an app would be better. It can send a reminder every morning.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: I agree. Paper diaries are always a problem. And the length of the study? Two weeks?

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: Actually, I wondered about four weeks. We'd see more patterns.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: I think that's too long. We hardly have enough time to analyse the data. One week would be easier.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: One week isn't enough to show a stable pattern, but four is more than your timetable allows. Two weeks is a good compromise. So keep your plan as it is.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: Okay. Two weeks it is.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Now, the memory test. What exactly will participants do?

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: We'll show them a list of twenty words for two minutes, and then they have to write down as many as they can remember the next morning.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Twenty words is sensible. Some students suggest a story or a set of pictures, but those are much harder to mark objectively. A word list gives you a simple score.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: We thought so too.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: One more thing about the words. Make sure they're all about the same length and equally common, otherwise some will be easier than others.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: We found a published list that has already been checked, so we'll use that.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: I think that's safer than choosing our own.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Exactly. And think about how participants will behave at night. Tell them not to review the words before bed.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: We'll put that in the instructions, in capital letters!

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: My main worry, though, isn't the type of test. It's the time of day. If some participants are tested at nine in the morning and others at four in the afternoon, you'll see a difference that has nothing to do with sleep.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: I hadn't thought of that. We did think about caffeine, because people who drink a lot of coffee might sleep badly.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Caffeine matters too, and you can ask about it in the diary. But it's something you can record. The testing time you must control. Test everyone in the same two-hour window.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: We can do that. Imogen has already booked the room for Tuesday and Thursday mornings.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Good. And is twenty participants enough? That's small.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: It is small, but we can only manage so many in the time. It's a limitation, and we'll say so.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: We could ask for thirty if the panel has enough volunteers.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Then ask for thirty and see how many reply.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Fine, as long as you say so. Now, what happens next? You have a lot to do before you start. Let's go through it. The ethics form is the first job. Nobody can recruit before the committee approves it.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: I've nearly finished it. I'll submit it by Friday.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Excellent. Then the recruitment email. Dev, you offered to write it?

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: Yes, I'll draft it tonight. Do I send it to everybody?

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: No, please don't. The department has a participant panel, and all recruitment messages go through it. They will send it for you, and they know who has already volunteered for other studies.

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: Right, I'll contact the panel, then.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: And the diary app. I'm afraid I don't know how to set one up. Ask Mr Brennan, the technician. He built one for a project last year, and he may be able to adapt it.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: I'll email him this afternoon. Dev, do you want me to print the consent forms as well?

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: There's no need. The forms will be online, and participants tick a box. It saves paper and the data is already in a file. Finally, the analysis. Have either of you used the statistics software?

transcript.speaker: Dev
transcript.text: Not properly. I've only watched a video.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the workshop on Monday afternoons. It's free, and it will save you hours later.

transcript.speaker: Imogen
transcript.text: We'll both go. Thanks very much, Dr Whitaker.

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: You're welcome. Dev: When do we need to start collecting data?

transcript.speaker: Dr Whitaker
transcript.text: Not before the middle of next month, because of the approval process. Come back and see me after the ethics decision, and we'll talk again.

sections.title: Bees in towns and cities
sections.context: You will hear an ecology lecturer talking about wild bees and honeybees in urban areas.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. In today's lecture I'd like to look at a question that surprises many people: why are some British cities better places for bees than the countryside? We usually imagine bees in meadows and orchards, not on busy streets. But research over the last fifteen years suggests the picture is more complicated.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let me start with some background. When people say bee, they usually mean the honeybee, the insect that lives in a hive and makes honey. But in Britain there are about 270 species of bee altogether. Only one of them is the honeybee. About twenty-five are bumblebees. All the rest, more than two hundred species, are quite different, and I'll come back to them in a moment.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Most of these remaining species are solitary bees. A solitary bee has no queen, no workers and no hive. Each female builds her own nest, usually a small tunnel in the soil or in a hollow stem, and lays her eggs there. They are often tiny, some of them smaller than a grain of rice, and they rarely sting. Many people have never noticed one, but they are some of our most important pollinators.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, what happens in cities? A few years ago, my own team carried out a survey of green spaces in Bristol. We counted bees in parks, gardens, cemeteries and allotments. The result that surprised us most was that the allotments had the greatest number of species. Allotments are small plots where people grow vegetables and flowers, and they are usually managed without heavy chemicals, so the soil is rich and undisturbed.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Why are cities so good? The key reason is variety. A farm field may contain a single crop, which flowers for only three weeks. A city garden, on the other hand, has hundreds of plants, chosen by hundreds of different owners. Something is in flower from early spring until the first frosts of the autumn. Bees need food over a long season, and a city can provide it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There is one more advantage that has been less discussed. Cities are warmer than the surrounding land, because buildings and roads store heat. In a large city, the temperature can be several degrees higher than in the nearby countryside. For a cold-blooded insect, that means an earlier start in the year and a longer flying season. There's also the question of chemicals. In gardens, people use far less spray per square metre than farmers do, and many city councils have stopped using weedkiller in their parks. This too makes a real difference.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That brings me to honeybees. In the last decade, keeping honeybees has become fashionable, and thousands of hives have appeared on the roofs of offices, hotels and even department stores. I think it's a wonderful hobby. It gets people interested in nature, and it produces honey of excellent quality. But there is a problem. If too many hives are placed in a small area, the honeybees compete with the wild bees for nectar, the sugary liquid that flowers produce. Honeybees are very efficient foragers, so they win the contest. In some parts of London, researchers have found that there are simply not enough flowers for all of them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So my advice to anyone thinking of getting a hive is to check how many are already nearby. And the best thing you can do for bees in general is not to keep them at all, but to help the wild ones.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: How might you do this? The first step is easy: leave a patch of your lawn uncut. Long grass and clover provide food, and it also gives shelter. Some of you may find this untidy, and your neighbours might complain, but the bees will thank you.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Second, provide places to nest. You can buy or make what is called a bee hotel. The best ones are made from pieces of bamboo, cut to the length of your hand and bundled together, with one end closed. Solitary bees move in and lay their eggs inside. Avoid hotels made from plastic, which can trap water and encourage mould.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Third, think about the plants you choose. Lavender is among the best, along with borage, and wild flowers like foxglove. Choose single flowers rather than the double ones in garden centres, because the double ones often contain little nectar.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, and most importantly, avoid pesticides. Even a small amount of chemical spray can kill a bee, or damage the nest that she has built. If you must deal with pests, use natural methods, such as encouraging ladybirds, or picking the insects off by hand.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: I'd also like you to remember that the evidence isn't perfect. Our survey covered a single year, and a different summer might give a different picture, so always be careful before drawing a general conclusion.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To summarise, cities are not the bee deserts that many people imagine. With the right care, they might become some of the most important refuges for these insects. In next week's lecture, we will move on to the question of butterflies, and ask whether a similar story can be told.
